In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: x86/mmu: Bug the VM if KVM attempts to walk more levels than the MMU has

Extend the "EFER.LMA && !CR4.PAE" check, which exists largely to guard
against KVM configuring a paging32 MMU with more than 2 levels of paging,
with a very explicit check for exactly that: that KVM isn't trying to walk
more levels of paging than the MMU template provides.  I.e. harden KVM
against all bugs that would cause KVM to generates accesses beyond the
bounds of guest_walker's arrays, regardless of how KVM ended up with the
misconfigured MMU.

Note, don't use w->cpu_role.base.level directly as the paging64 template
only provides two levels of page tables for PAE paging on 32-bit hosts, and
handles the third level by manually emulating the PDPTR access.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: nSVM: Ignore EFER.LMA if EFER.LME=0 when preparing L2 state

Force EFER.LMA=0 if EFER.LME=0 when preparing L2 state for VMRUN, i.e.
mimic real hardware's behavior of ignoring EFER.LMA if EFER.LME=0.  VMRUN
unfortunately allows the nonsensical combination, i.e. doesn't fail, but
KVM itself has an invariant EFER.LMA can be set et if and only if EFER.LME
is set.   Breaking that invariant can lead to a variety of issue,
particularly in MMU code that keys off EFER.LMA when determining whether to
emulate/virtualization 4/5-level paging versus PAE paging.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: SVM: Trigger new ASID allocation in both VMCBs on pCPU switch

When the pCPU where the VMCB was most recently used is switched, reset
the ASID generation in both VMCBs, triggering new ASID allocation for
the immediate VMRUN as well as the next VMRUN on the other VMCB.

The ASID is shared between vmcb01 and vmcb02, and gets flushed on every
nested transition. However, since pCPU tracking is done per VMCB, it is
possible for one VMCB to allocate a new ASID when migrated to a new
pCPU, and then the other VMCB reuses that ASID on the old pCPU. This can
result in the same ASID being used by multiple vCPUs on the old pCPU.

Example scenario:
- vCPU runs on pCPU A, vmcb01 is active, asid=1.
- vCPU migrates to pCPU B, vmcb01 pCPU changes, new asid=2.
- Another vCPU runs on pCPU A and allocates asid=2 as well.
- vCPU migrates back to pCPU A, and then switches to vmcb02 before it
  runs again with vmcb01.
- No pCPU switch is detected for vmcb02, so VMRUN is done with asid=2.
- Two vCPUs end up using asid=2 on the same pCPU.

Keep the VMCB dirtying to the active VMCB only. Clean bits are tracked
by a pCPU for each VMCB, so do not unnecessarily dirty a VMCB if its
pCPU does not change.

Additionally, initialize the tracked pCPU for vmcb02 to -1 on nested
enablement as hardening, so that a new ASID allocation is always
triggered when nested is disabled and re-enabled.

No performance regression was noticed when overcommitting L1 vCPUs in L0
(to force rescheduling), pinning L1 <-> L2 vCPUs, and running CPUID in a
tight loop bouncing between 2 vCPUs in L2.

An alternative (and perhaps more proper) fix would be tracking the ASID
per-VMCB instead (e.g. [1]). However, that's a more involved change, and
it would result in having different ASIDs for L1 and L2 without actually
properly maintaining them. It would probably work because all TLB
flushes target the current VMCB, and the other VMCB is always flushed on
nested transitions, but the code ends up in an arguably more fragile
state. Punt a proper clean fix to an incoming (and overdue) overhaul of
SVM's ASID usage [2].

[1] https://lore.kernel.org/lkml/20250205182402.2147495-2-yosry.ahmed@linux.dev
[2] https://lore.kernel.org/kvm/20260728003557.1136583-1-yosry@kernel.org

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

usb: gadget: fix refcount underflow in gadgetfs_bind() error path

gadgetfs_bind() calls get_dev() only on the success path, but
gadgetfs_unbind() called from the enomem error label unconditionally
calls put_dev().  When bind fails (e.g. ENOMEM), put_dev() fires
without a matching get_dev(), leaving the refcount unbalanced.

A subsequent close of the ep0 file descriptor calls dev_release() ->
put_dev() which hits zero and frees the object; then gadgetfs_kill_sb()
calls put_dev(the_device) again on the already-freed pointer, triggering
a refcount underflow and use-after-free.

Fix by calling get_dev() at the start of gadgetfs_bind(), before any
error path that invokes gadgetfs_unbind(), so the reference is always
balanced regardless of whether bind succeeds or fails.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ASoC: amd: ps: fix snd_acp63_remove() teardown ordering

The ACP IRQ handlers dereference the SoundWire, SoundWire DMA, and PDM
child platform devices, but snd_acp63_remove() unregisters them while
the interrupt is still held by devres, which frees it only after remove
returns. An interrupt in this window is a use-after-free.

Mask the ACP interrupt sources and call devm_free_irq() before the
first child device is unregistered. The masking goes through the new
acp_hw_ops->disable_interrupts callback, keeping the remove path
platform-agnostic. The interrupt line is shared, and acp_hw_deinit()
clears the sources only after the children are gone, which would
leave the line raised with no handler left to ack it. The window
predates the tagged refactor, which only reshaped the dereferences.

devm_free_irq() waits for in-flight handlers, but not for work the
hardirq has already queued: acp63_irq_handler() schedules
amd_sdw_irq_thread on the SoundWire manager. Draining that work in
the manager's remove path is a soundwire-side change and follows
separately.

This issue was found by an in-house static analysis tool.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ALSA: emux: Fix UAF of soundfont zones at note-on

snd_emux_note_on() looks up the matching zones via
snd_soundfont_search_zone(), which takes sflist->lock only during the
lookup and returns the raw zone pointers after releasing it.  The
caller then stores them in vp->zone without any protection.
Meanwhile, a concurrent SNDRV_EMUX_IOCTL_REMOVE_LAST_SAMPLES ioctl may
unlink and free those zones in snd_soundfont_remove_unlocked(); this
leads to a use-after-free in snd_emux_note_on(), and later at
accessing the cached vp->zone, e.g. in snd_emux_send_effect().

Fix it by holding sflist->lock in snd_emux_note_on() over the whole
zone lookup and voice setup, and let snd_soundfont_search_zone()
require the caller to hold the lock, instead.
snd_soundfont_lock_preset() takes sflist->lock for setting
presets_locked, so the removal path now syncs with the note-on finish.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.4, 10.2.8, 10.0.11, and 9.4.16, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role could create and share a metric alert that causes Analytics Workspace to run a malicious Search Processing Language (SPL) when another authenticated user opens a link to the alert. The malicious SPL could expose data, modify data, or disrupt services available in the affected session. 
The vulnerability is possible because Analytics Workspace does not fully neutralize metric alert names before including the names in SPL.
The vulnerability requires the attacker to phish the user by tricking them into opening a link that the attacker creates. The user who holds the "power" Splunk role should not be able to exploit the vulnerability at will.
For more information see Alerts in the Analytics Workspace (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/create-dashboards-and-reports/analytics-workspace/10.4/using-the-analytics-workspace/alerts-in-the-analytics-workspace) and Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role could craft a shared Classic Dashboard that runs arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) commands for another authenticated user. Exploitation requires the dashboard viewer to open the shared dashboard. The injected commands could access data available to the dashboard viewer, modify data available to the dashboard viewer, and partially disrupt Splunk Enterprise.
For more information see Add sparklines to search results (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/search/search-manual/10.6/calculate-statistics/add-sparklines-to-search-results), Configure dashboard permissions (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/create-dashboards-and-reports/simple-xml-dashboards/10.6/manage-and-share-dashboards/configure-dashboard-permissions), and SPL safeguards for risky commands (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.6/best-practices-for-splunk-platform-security/spl-safeguards-for-risky-commands) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role could add attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) to a shared dashboard. When another user opens the dashboard in Splunk Web, Splunk Enterprise could run the attacker-controlled SPL using the permissions of that dashboard viewer. The attacker-controlled SPL could expose stored credentials, modify indexed data, and reduce availability.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Enterprise does not neutralize special elements in search filter values before it builds optimized search jobs.
The vulnerability requires the attacker to phish the affected user by tricking them into initiating a request within their browser. The attacker should not be able to exploit the vulnerability at will.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role could store malicious Search Processing Language (SPL) in a shared dashboard. The malicious SPL could run using the permissions of the user who opened the dashboard and could access or modify data available to that user and disrupt Splunk Enterprise availability.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Enterprise does not preserve quoted search argument boundaries when it processes a dashboard search.
The vulnerability requires the attacker to phish the affected user by tricking them into initiating a request within their browser. The attacker, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role, should not be able to exploit the vulnerability at will.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a low-privileged user who holds the "power" Splunk role could inject arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) commands into a Classic Dashboard search. When another user opens the affected dashboard in Splunk Web, those injected commands execute with the viewing user's permissions, potentially allowing the low-privileged user to access stored credentials and write data to indexes.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Enterprise does not correctly escape user-supplied content when it rewrites a search, which lets the rewritten search include additional SPL commands.
The vulnerability requires another user to open the dashboard in Splunk Web. Consequently, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role should not be able to exploit the vulnerability at will.
For more information see SPL safeguards for risky commands (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.6/best-practices-for-splunk-platform-security/spl-safeguards-for-risky-commands) and Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.6/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.4, 10.2.8, 10.0.11, and 9.4.16, an unauthenticated user could craft a malicious link that, if opened by an authenticated user, executes arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) searches with the victim's permissions. 
Successful exploitation could allow the unauthenticated user to access or modify data, alter Splunk platform configurations, and disrupt operations available to the affected user.
The vulnerability is possible because the Portable Document Format (PDF) generation component processes request data before it rejects deprecated GET requests and does not apply SPL safeguards for risky commands to subsearches.
For more information see Generate PDFs of your reports and dashboards (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/create-dashboards-and-reports/reporting-manual/10.4/report-management/generate-pdfs-of-your-reports-and-dashboards) and SPL safeguards for risky commands (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/best-practices-for-splunk-platform-security/spl-safeguards-for-risky-commands) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.4, 10.2.8, 10.0.11, and 9.4.16, a low-privileged user who holds the "power" Splunk role could inject malicious content into a Splunk Web view. When another authenticated user opens the affected view in Splunk Web, the injected content executes unauthorized JavaScript code within the viewing user's browser session.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Web does not properly validate content in a view definition before rendering the view.
For more information see Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.2/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, and 10.0.12, a low-privileged user who holds the "power" Splunk role could overwrite shared application dashboard views with arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) commands. When another authenticated user opens an affected dashboard in Splunk Web, Splunk Enterprise executes the injected SPL using the viewing user's permissions, potentially allowing the low-privileged user to access or modify data available to that user.
The vulnerability is possible because the affected app grants the "power" Splunk role write access to shared dashboard views that should be writable only by the "admin" Splunk role.
The vulnerability is possible because the Splunk App for Splunk Observability Cloud grants the "power" Splunk role write access to shared dashboard views that should be writable only by the "admin" Splunk role

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, an authenticated user with edit permission for the container label on a pending approval could read an external-prompt capability through an Approval details Representational State Transfer (REST) API response and use it to view the prompt content, change the pending approval decision, and modify its action parameters.
The vulnerability is possible because an Approval details response exposes the external-prompt capability without checking approval ownership.
For more information see REST External Prompt (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/rest-api-reference/8.5.0/external-prompt-endpoints/rest-external-prompt) and Manage roles and permissions in Splunk SOAR (On-premises) (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/8.5.0/manage-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-users-and-accounts/manage-roles-and-permissions-in-splunk-soar-on-premises) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user that holds a role with the System Settings edit permission and restricted tenant access could modify settings for a tenant outside the role scope through the Representational State Transfer (REST) API. With this access, the user could expose confidential tenant environment values, alter tenant settings and automation behavior, or take the tenant out of operation.
The vulnerability is possible because the Tenant REST API checks the System Settings edit permission but does not enforce the tenant restrictions for the role before it updates the selected tenant.
For more information see Manage roles and permissions in Splunk SOAR (On-premises) (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/8.8.0/manage-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-users-and-accounts/manage-roles-and-permissions-in-splunk-soar-on-premises), Configure multiple tenants on your Splunk SOAR (On-premises) instance (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/8.7.0/configure-product-settings-for-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-instance/configure-multiple-tenants-on-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-instance), and REST Tenant (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/rest-api-reference/8.5.0/multi-tenancy-endpoints/rest-tenant) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user that holds a role with the Assets edit or delete permission and access to one or more tenants could change or delete assets assigned to other tenants through the Representational State Transfer (REST) API. With this access, the user could redirect connector traffic and expose the credentials and operational data associated with an asset, or disrupt integrations and data ingestion for other tenants.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR verifies the Assets edit or delete permission but does not verify that the user can access every tenant assigned to the target asset before Splunk SOAR changes or deletes the asset.
For more information see Manage roles and permissions in Splunk SOAR (On-premises) (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/8.8.0/manage-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-users-and-accounts/manage-roles-and-permissions-in-splunk-soar-on-premises), Configure multiple tenants on your Splunk SOAR (On-premises) instance (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/8.7.0/configure-product-settings-for-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-instance/configure-multiple-tenants-on-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-instance), Add and configure apps and assets to provide actions in Splunk SOAR (On-premises) (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/8.6.0/manage-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-apps-and-assets/add-and-configure-apps-and-assets-to-provide-actions-in-splunk-soar-on-premises), and Using the REST API reference for Splunk SOAR (On-premises) (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/rest-api-reference/8.5.0/using-the-splunk-soar-rest-api/using-the-rest-api-reference-for-splunk-soar-on-premises) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, an authenticated user that holds a role with the Apps edit, Containers edit, and Playbooks execute permissions could use the App Wizard to execute arbitrary code as the user account that runs Splunk SOAR. This could compromise the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the Splunk SOAR instance.
The vulnerability exists because the App Wizard does not validate user-supplied identifiers before incorporating them into generated connector code.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, an unauthenticated user could gain administrator privileges through a user account that receives an unintended role. A user that holds a role with permission to create or modify users and assign roles must assign the target account a role with a numeric name through the user-management Representational State Transfer (REST) API.
The vulnerability is possible because the API resolves a numeric role name as a role identifier instead of preserving the requested role name.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, an authenticated user that holds a role with the System Settings edit permission could execute arbitrary code on the host that runs Splunk SOAR.
The vulnerability is possible because the Representational State Transfer (REST) API accepts package references from untrusted sources and passes them to the dependency installer.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user that holds a role with the Apps edit permission could execute arbitrary code as the user account that runs Splunk SOAR by installing a malicious app.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR does not restrict app dependencies to validated binary packages before installing them.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user that holds a role with only the apps:edit permission could install a connector app that causes Splunk SOAR to write attacker-controlled files outside the app directory. This could let the user modify files used by Splunk SOAR and execute arbitrary code as the user account that runs Splunk SOAR.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR constructs the dependency installation command from app-supplied metadata without preventing that metadata from changing its arguments.
For more information see Manage roles and permissions in Splunk SOAR (On-premises) (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/8.8.0/manage-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-users-and-accounts/manage-roles-and-permissions-in-splunk-soar-on-premises) and Add and configure apps and assets to provide actions in Splunk SOAR (On-premises) (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/8.6.0/manage-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-apps-and-assets/add-and-configure-apps-and-assets-to-provide-actions-in-splunk-soar-on-premises) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user that holds a role with the System Settings edit permission could use a customer automation dependency to execute arbitrary code as the user account that runs Splunk SOAR.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR does not properly separate customer automation dependencies from trusted product code.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user that holds a role with the Apps edit permission could cause Splunk SOAR to execute arbitrary code on the host when the user validates an installed app.
The vulnerability is possible because the app validation workflow does not isolate untrusted code from the trusted environment.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, an authenticated user with repository edit access could cause Splunk SOAR to write files outside the configured repository, which lets the user modify files that the user account running Splunk SOAR can write to.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR does not require source control repository paths to remain inside the configured repository.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user that holds a role with the System Settings edit permission could use the Automation Dependency Wheel Representational State Transfer (REST) API to write arbitrary files outside the intended directory, which could lead to arbitrary code execution.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR does not restrict uploaded automation dependency wheel filenames to the intended storage directory.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user with local access to the affected host could obtain a live Splunk SOAR session token or decrypted asset configuration when another user starts an App Editor debug action.
The vulnerability is possible because App Editor debug actions expose sensitive runtime information to other local users on the affected host.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user who holds the "Observer" Splunk SOAR role could access a password-reset credential in a diagnostic log bundle and reset the password for an active local account.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR does not redact password-reset email bodies before it logs communications between product processes.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user that holds a role with the Playbooks view, edit, execute, and delete permissions could cause existing cross-repository playbook references to run attacker-controlled playbook code.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR can bind existing cross-repository playbook references to a different source control repository when a deleted repository name is reused.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user with access to the configured load balancer account could replace a load balancer helper that Splunk SOAR later runs with root privileges during cluster lifecycle operations. If a Splunk SOAR administrator performs a cluster lifecycle operation, Splunk SOAR could execute arbitrary code with root privileges on the load balancer.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR does not verify the integrity or ownership of the load balancer helper before running it with root privileges.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, an authenticated user with permission to edit and run playbooks could read or overwrite persisted data for playbook runs outside the authorized label, or ownership scope for that user. The affected data can include playbook inputs, prompt and block results, outputs, and secrets that playbooks save in run data. Overwriting the data could corrupt results that paused, scheduled, or parent playbook runs later use.
The vulnerability is possible because the playbook automation APIs do not bind data operations to the active playbook run.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, an authenticated user with permission to create and run playbooks could start child playbooks on containers outside the authorized label, or repository scope for that user. This could expose container data and affect automation outside that scope.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR does not bind the identity used to authorize the child playbook run to the parent playbook execution context.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, an operator of a configured identity provider could authenticate as an existing user associated with another configured identity provider. If that account has the "Administrator" Splunk SOAR role, the operator could control the Splunk SOAR deployment.
Splunk SOAR does not bind external user accounts to the identity provider that provisions them and authenticates accounts by username without verifying provider ownership.
The vulnerability requires more than one configured external identity provider with distinct trust domains and a target username that an operator of a configured identity provider can authenticate through a different provider.
For more information see Configure single sign-on authentication (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/8.7.0/manage-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-users-and-accounts/configure-single-sign-on-authentication-for-splunk-soar-on-premises) and Manage roles and permissions (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/8.8.0/manage-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-users-and-accounts/manage-roles-and-permissions-in-splunk-soar-on-premises) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.6.1, 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, an unauthenticated user could run arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) searches through RapidDiag task collection as an authenticated user. With this access, the user could read or modify data and configuration available to that authenticated user.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Enterprise accepts an empty shared secret when it authenticates RapidDiag task-collection requests.
For more information see Using RapidDiag (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/troubleshoot/9.3/contact-splunk-support/using-rapiddiag) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.16, a user who does not hold the "admin" or "power" Splunk roles could cause Splunk Enterprise to run arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) searches with elevated privileges through data model acceleration.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Enterprise does not correctly neutralize caller-supplied data model acceleration values before it places them into generated summarization searches.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 9.4.17, 10.0.12, 10.2.9, and 10.4.5, a user who does not hold the "admin" or "power" Splunk roles can configure a metric alert through the Representational State Transfer (REST) API that runs a search with elevated privileges. The vulnerability lets the user access or modify data and disrupt the Splunk Enterprise instance.
The vulnerability occurs because Splunk Enterprise does not enforce the required role-based authorization when it processes metric alert configuration through the REST API. Splunk Enterprise schedules the resulting search with elevated authorization and runs attacker-controlled search processing with that authorization.
For more information see About configuring role-based user access (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.6/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/about-configuring-role-based-user-access) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.16, a user who does not hold the "admin" or "power" Splunk roles could cause scheduled metric alert searches to run arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) commands and access credentials stored in cleartext. This requires at least one non-internal metric index on the instance.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Enterprise does not fully validate metric alert filter input before using it in a scheduled search.

IBM Guardium Data Protection 12.2 is vulnerable to missing authentication in the SharePoint S-TAP RelayService, allowing an unauthenticated network attacker to inject forged audit events and access the active monitoring policy.

IBM Guardium Data Protection 12.2 is vulnerable to a stack-based buffer overflow when processing a specially crafted PROXY protocol v1 header. A remote attacker can exploit this vulnerability to cause a denial of service or potentially execute arbitrary code.

IBM Guardium Data Protection 12.2 is vulnerable to local privilege escalation via the SUID-root podman_wrapper binary on the Collector appliance. A local attacker with low-privileged access to the Collector can exploit insufficient argument validation in the SUID binary to execute arbitrary commands as root, resulting in full compromise of the Collector appliance.

IBM Guardium Data Protection 12.2 is vulnerable to insecure deserialization in the SharePoint Tap MulticastTransceiver component. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability to execute arbitrary code on the affected system.

IBM Guardium Data Protection 12.2 is vulnerable to improper TLS certificate validation in the GDP Terraform provider, allowing a network attacker with a man-in-the-middle position to intercept sensitive credentials transmitted to the Guardium appliance.

IBM Guardium Data Protection 12.2 is vulnerable to SQL injection in the edge-controller component. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability to access or modify sensitive database information.

An uncontrolled recursion vulnerability exists in the LINE iOS app prior to version 26.19.0.

The Flex Message processing component does not adequately validate the structure of externally supplied message content.

As a result, an attacker who is able to send a crafted message to a victim could cause the application to crash when the message is received or displayed.

A server-side mitigation has been deployed that also protects existing iOS clients that have not been updated to version 26.19.0.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. When an administrator revokes tokens by setting a not-before revocation cutoff, Keycloak fails to enforce this boundary when processing User-Managed Access (UMA) grant requests using ID token claims. An authenticated remote user with an active session can submit a previously revoked ID token to receive a fresh Requesting Party Token (RPT). This flaw allows an attacker to bypass token revocation and retain unauthorized access to protected resources.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. When processing token requests using the User-Managed Access (UMA) grant, Keycloak fails to verify whether a target client or resource server is enabled before issuing an authorization token. An authenticated remote user can exploit this flaw to obtain valid Requesting Party Tokens (RPTs) for disabled clients, bypassing administrative access controls and permissions restrictions.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. The Account API endpoint for sharing resources fails to verify whether owner-managed access is enabled and accepts permission scopes not assigned to the resource. An authenticated user can exploit this vulnerability to generate pre-granted permission tickets, causing Keycloak to bypass policy evaluation and issue access tokens with unauthorized scopes.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. When a client application enforces step-up authentication or multi-factor authentication (MFA) via a minimum authentication level, Keycloak fails to apply this requirement to login sessions initiated through the credential reset endpoint. An attacker who possesses a user's initial credentials (such as a password) can navigate from the reset interface back to the standard login form and authenticate without completing the required second factor. This flaw allows an attacker to obtain valid access tokens and gain unauthorized access to protected services without satisfying mandatory security controls.

A vulnerability was detected in smartalock wireguard-lwip up to cfba91666590e86bd67842c71cedf9a423be823a. This affects the function wireguard_generate_unique_index of the file src/wireguard.c of the component Session Index Allocator. The manipulation of the argument receiver_index results in allocation of resources. The attack is only possible with local access. The project was informed of the problem early through an issue report but has not responded yet.

A security flaw has been discovered in sofastack sofa-bolt up to 1.6.12. Affected by this issue is the function HessianSerializer.deserialize of the file src/main/java/com/alipay/remoting/serialization/HessianSerializer.java of the component Hessian2 Deserialization. Performing a manipulation results in allocation of resources. The attack can be initiated remotely. The vendor was contacted early about this disclosure but did not respond in any way.

A vulnerability has been found in sumiie24 School-Management-System up to d946d649c7c95e101fc5679ecd91999533bb10d7. The affected element is an unknown function of the file parent_Registration.php. Such manipulation of the argument student_reg leads to sql injection. The attack can be executed remotely. The exploit has been disclosed to the public and may be used. This product implements a rolling release for ongoing delivery, which means version information for affected or updated releases is unavailable.

A weakness has been identified in sofastack sofa-bolt up to 1.6.12. This impacts the function initSSLContext of the file src/main/java/com/alipay/remoting/connection/AbstractConnectionFactory.java of the component TLS Stack. Executing a manipulation can lead to certificate with host mismatch. The attack may be performed from remote. This attack is characterized by high complexity. The exploitability is said to be difficult. The vendor was contacted early about this disclosure but did not respond in any way.

A security vulnerability has been detected in rajesh2211 Doctor-Appointment-System up to ee974dcf4c50da85e6ea026e27f4370e9468b3cc. Affected is an unknown function of the file AppointmentSystem/AppointmentSystem/Connectivity.php of the component Login. The manipulation of the argument User leads to sql injection. It is possible to initiate the attack remotely. The exploit has been disclosed publicly and may be used. This product is using a rolling release to provide continious delivery. Therefore, no version details for affected nor updated releases are available.

A vulnerability was detected in WebKul QloApps up to 1.8.0. Affected by this vulnerability is the function postProcessDownload/installTheme of the file controllers/admin/AdminModulesController.php of the component Archive Import. The manipulation results in path traversal. It is possible to launch the attack remotely. The exploit is now public and may be used. The vendor was contacted early about this disclosure but did not respond in any way.
PowerLink developed by Neotroni Lighting has a SQL Injection vulnerability, allowing unauthenticated remote attackers to inject arbitrary SQL commands to read database contents.

A flaw was found in Hawtio. An authenticated remote attacker can cause a Denial of Service (DoS) by sending a specially crafted request URI to monitored endpoints. The FlightRecordingDownloadFacade servlet filter uses an inefficient regular expression pattern that causes catastrophic backtracking when processing certain long requests. This issue leads to excessive CPU utilization, causing handling threads to hang and degrading service availability.

NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM for any platform contains a vulnerability where a user may cause a race condition by running concurrent requests. A successful exploit of this vulnerability may lead to data tampering.

NVIDIA VIRTIO-Net for Bluefield contains a vulnerability in Virtio-Net where a VM user may cause a Write-What-Where condition by crafted message. A successful exploit of this vulnerability may lead to Code Execution in Virtio-Net scope.

Multiple products produced by Ruijie Networks Co., Ltd. contain an OS command injection vulnerability that may lead to arbitrary OS commands being executed by an attacker with the administrative privilege.

A flaw has been found in hrshadhin CloudSchool up to 3.0.1. Affected by this issue is the function PublicController.checkSanity4Student of the file app/Http/Controllers/Backend/PublicController.php of the component Student Data Access Check. This manipulation of the argument student_id causes authorization bypass. The attack can be initiated remotely. The exploit has been published and may be used. The project was informed of the problem early through an issue report but has not responded yet.

A vulnerability has been found in hrshadhin CloudSchool up to 3.0.1. This affects the function EventController@store of the file app/Http/Controllers/Backend/EventController.php of the component Admin Content Management. Such manipulation of the argument data leads to cross site scripting. The attack can be launched remotely. The exploit has been disclosed to the public and may be used. The project was informed of the problem early through an issue report but has not responded yet.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. The OpenID Connect (OIDC) logout endpoint continues to honor post-logout redirect rules for disabled clients rather than rejecting the requests. If a disabled client retains permissive redirect configurations, a remote attacker can exploit this issue by supplying an arbitrary redirection target in a logout request, leading to an open redirect that can be used in phishing attacks.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. When evaluating access permissions, Keycloak Authorization Services improperly matches resource paths containing wildcard file extensions by evaluating only the file extension suffix and ignoring configured path prefixes. An authenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by requesting a restricted resource that shares a file extension with a more permissive resource, leading to an authorization bypass and unintended access to protected data.

A flaw was found in crun. When copying files onto a tmpfs mounted with tmpcopyup, crun opens the destination a second time by name. A container that shares a writable volume with the container being created can change that path between the two lookups, so crun copies image files onto host files, including files under /proc/sys.

An improper export control defect in ChatEventDispatchActivity (com.vivo.agent.business.chatmode.activity.ChatEventDispatchActivity) of Vivo Assistant allows a local malicious application to execute voice commands without user interaction via a crafted Intent, which may lead to unauthorized phone calls, SMS sending, access to private data such as location and calendar entries, and modification of system settings

A vulnerability was found in ByteDance Lark Desktop 8.0.0.14. This vulnerability affects the function FUN_18001b770/FUN_18001ba40 in the library backend.dll. Performing a manipulation of the argument day results in signed to unsigned conversion error. The attack needs to be approached locally. The exploit has been made public and could be used. The vendor was contacted early about this disclosure but did not respond in any way.

A vulnerability was identified in hasan-py Hayroo up to fd0fbe763153f72bfaa04ed1e1e4a1bb6f7c61df. Affected by this issue is the function Product.deleteImages of the file server/controller/products.js of the component Image Deletion Handler. The manipulation leads to path traversal. The attack may be initiated remotely. The exploit is publicly available and might be used. This product uses a rolling release model to deliver continuous updates. In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

assoc_array: keep gc's cleanup out of the live tree on allocation failure

assoc_array_gc() builds a copy of the tree.  Where the copy reaches a
shortcut, it allocates the copy of the shortcut with kmalloc_flex(),
fills it with memcpy(), links it into the new tree, and only then
allocates the copy of the node after it.  The memcpy() leaves the new
shortcut's next_node pointing at the old tree's node, so if that second
allocation fails, the cleanup, assoc_array_destroy_subtree() on the new
tree, follows the new shortcut into the old tree, and the BUG_ON() on
the old node's back pointer fires.

Allocate the node first, and the shortcut once the node exists, freeing
the node again if the shortcut cannot be allocated.  A copied shortcut
is then only linked into the new tree when the copy of its node is there
to follow it.  Nothing else changes: with no allocation failing, the
trees gc builds are the same as before.

Found by a userspace test that makes each allocation of each operation
fail in turn.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

assoc_array: don't chain a new shortcut onto an existing one

When a full node's leaves and the new key all share the node's segment,
assoc_array_insert_into_terminal_node() replaces the node with a
shortcut to a pair of new nodes.  If the node is itself the target of a
shortcut, the new shortcut is installed as that shortcut's next node,
and a shortcut leading to a shortcut is something nothing expects:
assoc_array_walk() indexes the second one as a node, and
assoc_array_apply_edit() hits the BUG_ON() in the loop that adjusts
nr_leaves_on_branch, on that same insertion.

Deletion gets a node there.  When the subtree below a shortcut shrinks
enough, assoc_array_delete() collapses it into one node below the
shortcut, and the leaves it collects can all share that node's segment.
The next key that shares it too takes this path.  Eighteen insertions
and a deletion are enough: sixteen keys that agree on bits 0-11, one
that leaves them at bit 8 and is deleted again, and one more that agrees
with the sixteen.

Have the new shortcut replace the one in front of the node as well.
assoc_array_insert_shortcut() gives it that shortcut's back pointer and
parent slot, so the caller installs it where that one was, and excises
the old shortcut along with the node, which takes a second entry in
excised_meta[].  The new shortcut's index key comes from the new key up
to the new skip level, so it covers what the old one did.

Found by a userspace test doing random insertions and deletions on keys
that share long prefixes; a targeted case builds a shortcut, deletes
down to the collapse and inserts one more key.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

iommufd/iova_bitmap: Ensure that iova_bitmap_set() handles the full IOVA

Generally userspace is going to step the dirty bitmap through the IOVA
space. However if the bitmap ends in the middle of a large PTE this is
problematic. The first step will clear the dirty bit and report dirty to
the end of its bitmap while the second step will see the clear'd dirty and
report clean for the start of the bitmap. If it happens this ends up
losing dirties.

Further this function is missing bounds checking so if this does happen
ther is a good chance it will write memory beyond what the userspace was
expecting.

Return an error code if this illegal condition happens.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: release a removed xattr node in roll-forward recovery

When xattrs shrink enough to fit in the inline xattr area,
write_all_xattrs() truncates the xattr node and clears i_xattr_nid. If
the file is then fsynced without a checkpoint, only the inode block is
written, with i_xattr_nid of 0.

Roll-forward recovery starts from the checkpointed inode, whose
i_xattr_nid still points to the old xattr node.
f2fs_recover_inline_xattr() copies only the inline xattr area, and
f2fs_update_inode() writes the old i_xattr_nid back. So the inode keeps
the stale xattr node:

 - The node block is never released, and fsck reports "nonzero bytes in
   xattr space after end of list".
 - If the inline xattr list ends exactly at the end of the inline area,
   its terminator is read from the stale node, and the removed xattrs
   come back after recovery.

When the fsynced inode has no xattr node but the checkpointed one has,
release the old xattr node as truncate_node() does: check its block
address, invalidate the block and drop its node cache, which may still
be dirty.

"f2fs_io shutdown 1") triggers below kernel BUG:

  f2fs_outplace_write_data+0x192/0x340
  f2fs_do_write_data_page+0xc57/0x1880
  f2fs_write_single_data_page+0xda9/0x15a0

  process_one_work+0x925/0x1600
  worker_thread+0x60a/0xff0
  kthread+0x35f/0x460
  ret_from_fork+0x474/0x7e0
  ret_from_fork_asm+0x1a/0x30
  </TASK>

The BUG is f2fs_bug_on(sbi, curseg->next_blkoff >= BLKS_PER_SEG(sbi))
in f2fs_allocate_data_block(), next_blkoff was 512.

The root cause is a race in between atomic write commit and shutdown
as below:

Thread A (commit atomic write)  Thread B (shutdown)        Thread C (writeback)
- f2fs_ioc_commit_atomic_write
 - f2fs_commit_atomic_write
  - __f2fs_commit_atomic_write
   - __replace_atomic_write_block
    - f2fs_replace_block
     - __f2fs_replace_block
                                - f2fs_ioc_shutdown
                                 - f2fs_do_shutdown
                                 : F2FS_GOING_DOWN_METASYNC
                                  - f2fs_sync_fs
                                                           - f2fs_write_single_data_page
                                                           : pass f2fs_cp_error() check
                                  - f2fs_stop_checkpoint
                                  : set CP_ERROR_FLAG
      - change_curseg
       - reset_curseg
       : curseg->segno = new_segno
       : curseg->alloc_type = SSR
       : curseg->next_blkoff = __next_free_blkoff()
         which is BLKS_PER_SEG if there is no free
         slot in new_segno
       - f2fs_get_sum_cache
       : return -EIO due to f2fs_cp_error()
      : return error w/o restoring curseg
     : goto out_unlock, skip restoring
       old segno, blkoff and alloc_type
                                                            - f2fs_do_write_data_page
                                                             - f2fs_outplace_write_data
                                                              - do_write_block
                                                               - f2fs_allocate_data_block
                                                               : curseg->segno is valid
                                                               : f2fs_bug_on(next_blkoff >=
                                                                 BLKS_PER_SEG)

Since commit 86f33603f8c5 ("f2fs: handle errors of
f2fs_get_meta_page_nofail"), change_curseg() can fail after the curseg
has already been switched to the new segment, then the curseg is left
in an inconsistent state: it points to a segment which may have no
free slot, its summary block is zeroed, and the caller can not restore
it. Subsequent block allocation on the curseg will trigger the BUG.
Moreover, the writeback thread dies with curseg_lock, curseg_mutex and
sentry_lock held, so the commit, shutdown and other I/O threads hang
in D state.

Since change_curseg() only fails once CP_ERROR_FLAG is set, no
checkpoint will be committed afterward, let's invalidate the curseg via
reset_curseg_fields() on failure, as new_curseg() does for -ENOSPC,
then f2fs_allocate_data_block() will fail with -ENOSPC on the curseg
instead of triggering BUG, and do_write_block() can handle the error
since CP_ERROR_FLA

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nvme-tcp: Validate the queue state under the queue lock in the address attribute

Reading the "address" sysfs attribute calls kernel_getsockname() on the
admin queue socket, which can race with the queue teardown during
connection error recovery: a reader can observe NVME_TCP_Q_LIVE set,
then block on the queue lock while nvme_tcp_free_queue() releases the
socket and clears queue->sock without holding the lock.  Once the
reader acquires the lock it dereferences the NULL socket pointer.

Commit 76d54bf20cdc ("nvme-tcp: don't access released socket during
error recovery") had the queue liveness check inside the lock.
Commit 782373ba2766 ("nvme: tcp: avoid race between queue_lock lock
and destroy") moved it back out because the lock itself is destroyed
in nvme_tcp_free_queue(), so a reader arriving late trips
mutex_destroy().

Check the queue liveness inside the queue lock, and clear queue->sock
under the same lock.  The teardown clears NVME_TCP_Q_LIVE under the
lock well before the socket is released, so a reader either sees the
bit cleared or a socket that cannot be released while it holds the
lock.  To also close the lock lifetime race, the queue locks are now
owned by the controller: they are initialized with the queue array and
only destroyed when the controller is freed, which cannot happen while
a sysfs attribute read is still in progress.  The queue count is
computed by the NVME_TCP_OPT_NR_QUEUES() macro from the original
connect options for both initialization and destruction, as reconnects
may shrink ctrl->queue_count.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: fix to avoid potential reference count leak in do_garbage_collect()

In do_garbage_collect(), we have reserved reference counts on summary cache
of all segments, once gc_thread encounter freezing, we need to release all
reference counts.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: arm64: vgic: Stop the target vcpu when disabling LPIs

Disabling LPIs is pretty nasty, as it directly messes with the AP list
of the affected CPU, which could be running... This has the potential to
lead to really bad behaviours, and we should not be doing that.

Take example on the way the Active state is handled and simply pause the
the vcpu so that we are sure it is in a quiescent state, and the state be
safely manipulated.

Nobody has any expectation of performance for this anyway.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: bound the SIT/NAT bitmaps by the checkpoint pack

sit_ver_bitmap_bytesize and nat_ver_bitmap_bytesize are used as memcpy
lengths into and out of sbi->ckpt, which is sized from cp_payload alone,
and nothing compares either length against that allocation.

sanity_check_ckpt() has checked these two fields since c77ec61ca0a4, which
added them after a crafted image overran build_sit_info(). That check ties
each length to a segment count; it never compares either against the
allocation, which is the half this adds.

Mounting over-reads in build_sit_info() and build_node_manager(), and the
first checkpoint writes the same lengths back through the same pointers,
so the over-read's contents reach the on-disk checkpoint. An unmount is
enough; the filesystem does not have to be used.

Bound both ends the way __bitmap_ptr() lays them out. The three branches
differ, so a single sum of the two lengths would still admit a small
overflow when cp_payload is non-zero.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: return -EIO for a lost inode block after cp_error

After cp_error, dirty node caches are dropped without being written.
If such an inode was never written, its NAT entry is still NEW_ADDR,
and reading its inode block returns -ENOENT.

f2fs_get_dnode_of_data() passes that -ENOENT up, and callers take it
as a hole. Since the inode block is missing, the next offset can only
advance one block, so fiemap walks block by block up to maxbytes,
about 2^30 blocks, while holding the inode lock. It took hours in a
power-off recovery test after shutdown and blocked unlink and umount
on the file.

Return -EIO instead of -ENOENT when the inode block itself is missing
after cp_error or shutdown. A missing direct or indirect node is still
reported as -ENOENT.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: zone: fix to avoid bio split on sequential zone

In the block layer, bio_split_to_limits() splits a bio if it exceeds
any underlying queue limits:
1. queue_max_sectors: Splits bios larger than the transfer limit. This
   limit is set by the device driver/DMA controller (max_hw_sectors) and
   device-mapper targets. When flushing dirty pages (governed by VFS
   writeback_chunk_size() and f2fs nr_pages_to_skip()), f2fs merges
   contiguous pages into bios up to 512KB (1024 sectors) or more without
   checking queue_max_sectors, which will be split if the device or DM
   target enforces a smaller limit.
2. queue_max_segments: Splits bios exceeding scatter-gather segment
   limits. f2fs allocates bios with up to 256 pages, exceeding the
   128-segment limit of DM targets (dm-default-key/dm-crypt) if pages
   are discontiguous.
3. chunk_sectors: Splits bios crossing chunk/zone boundaries. In f2fs,
   section_size strictly matches zone_size, and block allocation never
   spans across section boundaries, so bios never cross chunk_sectors.

Crucially, when bio_split_to_limits() splits a bio, bio_submit_split()
submits the tail half via submit_bio_noacct() before returning the head
half to the caller. On a sequential zoned device, this causes the tail
bio to arrive at the zone write plug before the head:

  dm-3: zone 7: prepare_bio wp mismatch: bio sector 30720 offset 2048
  != wp_offset 248, len 248

The write plug rejects the out-of-order tail with BLK_STS_IOERR, causing
f2fs_stop_checkpoint() and remounting the filesystem read-only:

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wifi: rtw88: usb: bound what the driver feeds the after-DTIM queue

Frames routed to the high queue are transmitted right after DTIM beacons
only, inside the ATIM window, while they wait in the shared TX page pool.
The driver puts no limit on how many it hands over, so as long as one
station dozes, any sustained broadcast or multicast traffic outruns the
drain and empties the pool: measured on an RTL8822BU AP with a single
client in power save and ~40 frames/s of mDNS chatter, the free page
count at 0x240 goes from 1803 to 16 in about 100 seconds and stays there
for as long as the traffic lasts. From that point every other transmit
queues behind the backlog, authentication responses arrive too late for
anyone to join, and the reserved page download fails ("error beacon
valid"). The AP keeps beaconing and only a reboot recovers.

Feed the high queue through a small budget that refills below the
measured drain rate (about 3 frames per DTIM, ~15/s at dtim_period 2 on
the default 2 TU ATIM window); whatever exceeds the budget leaves on its
access category queue right away. The high queue backlog is now bounded
by the burst size under any load, so the page pool cannot run dry, at
the price that a dozing station may miss part of a broadcast storm.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wifi: rtw88: usb: route bmc frames via the high queue only for DTIM delivery

In AP mode every broadcast and multicast data frame is routed to
TX_DESC_QSEL_HIGH, the after-DTIM queue, whether or not anybody is
asleep. The firmware drains that queue at beacon pace, a dozen or so
frames per second measured on RTL8822BU, while one associated client's
mDNS/SSDP chatter alone exceeds that. The excess accumulates inside
the chip until the shared TX page pool is exhausted (measured: 14 of
1803 pages left). From that point every host-sourced frame queues
behind the backlog: authentication responses reach the air seconds
after the client has given up, so no station can associate anymore,
and the beacon reserved-page download fails the BCN_VALID poll
("error beacon valid") because it needs pages from the same pool. The
AP keeps beaconing, so the failure looks like a silent RX stall and
only a reboot recovers.

mac80211 already decides when after-DTIM delivery is needed: it sets
IEEE80211_TX_CTL_SEND_AFTER_DTIM on bmc frames only while at least one
station is actually dozing. Honor that instead of routing
unconditionally: flagged frames keep going through the high queue with
the MORE_DATA and HGQMD handling introduced by commit 076f786a0ae1
("wifi: rtw88: Fix AP mode incorrect DTIM behavior"), everything else
leaves at line rate through the AC queues. This partially reverts the
usb.c hunk of that commit, whose unconditional routing is what lets
the backlog build up.

On a bench AP (USB2, 20 MHz, WPA2, hostapd, a Windows client driven
through disconnect/reconnect cycles): reconnects fail 0/5 on RTL8822BU
and 0/3 on RTL8821CU before this change, and pass 10/10 and 5/5 with
it, with the page pool staying healthy and no beacon errors logged.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/shmem: honour F_SEAL_EXEC when an ACL is set

The owner of a memfd sealed with F_SEAL_EXEC can still change its
execute bits by setting a POSIX access ACL. With CONFIG_TMPFS_POSIX_ACL,
this lets an unprivileged owner make a non-executable memfd executable,
bypassing vm.memfd_noexec=2.

simple_set_acl() updates i_mode directly, bypassing the seal check in
shmem_setattr(). Add shmem_set_acl() to check the resulting mode. Share
the F_SEAL_EXEC check with shmem_setattr() using memfd_check_seals_mode()
in include/linux/memfd.h.

Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Chris Mason in private.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/userfaultfd: only allocate anon_vma in CoW mappings

find_vma_and_prepare_anon() can end up allocating an anon_vma in VMAs that
are not CoW mappings, which is wrong.

If we have a MAP_SHARED R/O file mapped, we lack VM_SHARED (but do have
VM_MAYSHARE) and lack VM_MAYWRITE.

While uffd later rejects such mappings (uffd registration requires
VM_MAYWRITE, see comment in validate_dst_vma) find_vma_and_prepare_anon()
still wrongly allocates an anon vma before it validates the vma.

This in turn later confuses copy_page_range()->vma_needs_copy() such
that we end up calling copy_hugetlb_page_range() with ranges that
actually do not contain *any* per-pagetable information that would
require copying, which is the basis for PMD-table sharing in the first
place.

copy_hugetlb_page_range() should not have to worry about shared
PMD tables at all: it doesn't make any sense to copy page tables that are
shared, as they can be fully recreated later. Ending up in the function
with shareable page tables is the real issue.

If a destination PMD table is shared in copy_hugetlb_page_range(), it
might get concurrently unshared as we are not holding relevant
locks, resulting in us using a page table that is no longer mapped and
possibly freed after calling:

	dst_pte = huge_pte_alloc(dst, dst_vma, addr, sz);

To fix it, do not allocate an anon_vma in non-CoW mappings and add a
safety guard to copy_hugetlb_page_range(), making sure that we never
end up messing with shared PMD tables in there.

Before commit 867a43a34ff8a ("userfaultfd: use per-vma locks in userfaultfd
operations") we would always validate the VMA before allocating an
anon_vma, and consequently never wrongly allocate an anon_vma.

As uffd_lock_vma() is part of the same lookup machinery and
also contains a misleading VM_SHARED check, change that one as well
directly for consistency.

A follow-up cleanup will stop taking the hugetlb_vma_lock_read(src_vma)
lock in copy_hugetlb_page_range() entirely. Further, the usage of
VM_SHARED in userfaultfd code should be cleaned up later to focus on
CoW vs. non-CoW mappings.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

platform/chrome: cros_usbpd_notify: Only use drvdata when parent is GOOG0004

cros_usbpd_notify_probe_acpi() takes the EC device pointer from
dev_get_drvdata(dev->parent) and assumes it is a struct cros_ec_device.
That only holds when GOOG0003 is a child of GOOG0004. On older devices
without that hierarchy, such as Google Nami, GOOG0003 and GOOG0004 are
siblings under the ACPI EC (PNP0C09):

  PNP0C09:00 (acpi-ec)
  |-- GOOG0003:00 (cros-usbpd-notify-acpi)
  `-- GOOG0004:00 (cros_ec_lpcs)

Before commit db65a06d10b3 ("ACPI: EC: Convert the driver to a platform
one") the parent platform device had no driver data, so the driver
warned and continued without an EC pointer, as intended for these
devices. Since that commit the ACPI EC driver stores its struct acpi_ec
there, so the driver treats a struct acpi_ec as a struct cros_ec_device
and calls cros_ec_cmd() on it for every USB-C PD host event. Plugging
or unplugging a charger then intermittently oopses, followed by soft
lockups and a hung system:

  BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: ffffffff9cf03220
  #PF: supervisor write access in kernel mode
  Hardware name: Google Nami/Nami, BIOS  09/19/2019
  Workqueue: kacpi_notify acpi_os_execute_deferred
  RIP: 0010:native_queued_spin_lock_slowpath+0x29d/0x330
  Call Trace:
   _raw_spin_lock_irqsave+0x59/0x80
   __mutex_lock.constprop.0+0x129/0x930
   cros_ec_cmd_xfer+0x2a/0xf0 [cros_ec_proto]
   cros_ec_cmd_xfer_status+0x1a/0x90 [cros_ec_proto]
   cros_ec_cmd+0xb7/0x140 [cros_ec_proto]
   cros_usbpd_get_event_and_notify+0x42/0xc0 [cros_usbpd_notify]
   acpi_ev_notify_dispatch+0x4e/0x70
   acpi_os_execute_deferred+0x1a/0x30

Only read the parent's driver data when the parent's ACPI node is
GOOG0004, and otherwise continue without an EC pointer. While at it,
drop the reference taken by fwnode_get_parent().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sctp: re-point retained control chunks on association migration

sctp_sock_migrate() transfers DATA chunk ownership but leaves retained
control chunks pointing at the old socket. A later retransmission can
therefore access the socket after it has been freed.

Extend the migration walk to cover retained control chunks and use
sctp_control_set_owner_w() to assign their new owner. Reuse the DATA
ownership check so each chunk is processed once per pass, even when it
is reachable through multiple lists or retained pointers.

Preserve a control chunk's existing authentication key across migration
so its final release can still generate SCTP_AUTH_FREE_KEY when needed.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sctp: hold shkey across socket migration

sctp_sock_migrate() transfers queued DATA skbs from the old socket to the
new one. skb_orphan() invokes sctp_wfree() during that transfer and drops
the skb-owned shared-key reference.

If userspace has removed that key from the association, this can be the
final reference. The following sctp_set_owner_w() then dereferences the
freed chunk->shkey while trying to take the new owner reference.

Take a temporary shared-key reference before orphaning the skb and release
it after the new owner has taken its reference. This preserves the selected
authentication key throughout the ownership transfer.

Bug found and triaged by OpenAI Security Research and
validated by Trail of Bits.
